extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, and patent practitioners considering PTAB proceedings or ex parte appeals (U.S. practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical procedural guidance on PTAB composition, AIA trial types/standards (IPR/PGR/CBM), and the ex parte appeal process (steps, deadlines, briefing requirements, oral hearing, and Board decision outcomes) before the U.S. Patent Trial and Appeal Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of PTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board is created by statute (35 U.S.C. § 6) — that statute mandates the Board’s duties, composition, qualifications for membership, and panel form of decision-making (appeals, derivation proceedings, post-grant reviews, and inter partes reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB decisions are made by panels; statutory foundation governs duties, composition, qualifications. (Slide: 'The Board is created by statute (35 U.S.C. § 6)')

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory members of the Board (35 U.S.C. § 6(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall be in the Office a Patent Trial and Appeal Board. The Director, the Deputy Director, the Commissioner for Patents, the Commissioner for Trademarks, and the administrative patent judges shall constitute the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists the statutory offices that constitute the PTAB as required by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Patent Judges staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: PTAB includes: Chief Judge (1), Deputy Chief Judge (1), Vice Chief Judges (5), Lead Judges (31), Judges (235). Patent attorneys, law clerks, paralegals, administrators, and support staff assist the judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational staffing and supporting roles; indicates technical and legal staffing resources available to adjudicate appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of PTAB proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings before the Board include: Appeals in ex parte patent applications; Appeals in ex parte and inter partes reexamination proceedings; Interferences; Inter partes reviews (IPR); Post-grant reviews (PGR); Covered business method reviews (CBM); Derivations (DER).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the range of proceedings handled by PTAB so practitioners can choose appropriate pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent behind AIA trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Faster and cheaper alternative to district court litigation to challenge patent validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider securing counsel because the proceedings can be complex; AIA trials provide an administrative alternative to federal court validity challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties to AIA trials — roles and burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner = third party who files challenge against a patent and carries legal burdens throughout proceeding; Patent owner can choose whether to defend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies who bears the burdens in AIA trials and strategic considerations for patent owners vs petitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of AIA trials (enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes review (IPR); Post grant review (PGR); Covered business method review (CBM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic categorization of AIA trial types; each has different availability windows and grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of AIA trials (timing and CBM definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR: from 9 months after patent grant throughout the life of the patent. PGR: from patent grant through 9 months. CBM: same as PGR, but must be a 'covered business method' patent (claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing or other operations used in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service) and does not include 'technological inventions'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified time windows to determine availability; CBM has subject-matter eligibility limitations (financial/business-method focus, excludes tech inventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of grounds in petition
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR: only on § 102 and § 103 grounds, and only on basis of prior art consisting of patents and printed publications. PGR/CBM: on any grounds for invalidity (except best mode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations on admissible grounds differ by proceeding type — choose proceeding accordingly based on available grounds and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for initiating review (institution threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR: 'a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail' with respect to at least one challenged claim. CBM/PGR: 'more likely than not that at least one claim is unpatentable' or the petition raises 'a novel or unsettled legal question that is important to other patents or applications'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different institution standards: IPR (reasonable likelihood) is lower than PGR/CBM (more likely than not) except when novel legal questions justify institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof in AIA trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a lower standard than the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard typically required to prevail in district courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of AIA trial if instituted
rubrics_metrics.description: Final decision issued within 12 months of institution; can extend by 6 months, but only for 'good cause'. Generally, entire process (petition → termination or final decision) will take 18 months or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect relatively expedited schedules compared to district court; extensions are limited and must be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of an ex parte appeal to the PTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative to continuing prosecution before the Examiner; consideration of the application 'as is', not a forum for making substantive amendments or submitting new evidence; generally results in a decision affirming or reversing the Examiner — the PTAB will not issue a patent. 'We simply review the Examiner’s decision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat ex parte appeal as a chance to add new matter; the appeal reviews the Examiner's positions as presented in the prosecution record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel review and legal environment for ex parte appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Review by a 'fresh pair of eyes,' namely a panel of at least three administrative patent judges who have technical backgrounds and are lawyers; a more formal, legal environment within the Office (legal briefing, optional oral argument before panel of judges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect legalistic proceedings with written briefs and optional oral hearing before a three-judge panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal environment: counsel and fairness practices
rubrics_metrics.description: No requirement to have a lawyer, but often a good idea. The Office cannot provide counsel on your behalf. The PTAB treats every appellant equally; to assure an appellant gets a fair shake, judges may provide more explanation if appellant needs it, and judges focus on the facts and evidence and can be more lenient on procedural formalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pro se appellants are accommodated to some degree, but legal representation is recommended; use PTAB resources available online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex Parte Appeal Process — nine-step overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Adverse Decision of the Examiner; Step 2: Notice of Appeal; Step 3: Appeal Brief; Step 4: Examiner’s Answer; Step 5: Appeal Forwarding Fee + Reply Brief (optional) + Request for Oral Hearing (optional); Step 6: Oral Hearing (if requested); Step 7: Board decision; Step 8: Request for rehearing (optional); Step 9: Decision on rehearing (if requested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the sequential process and applicable CFR and MPEP citations (37 C.F.R. §§ 41.31-54; MPEP §§ 1204-1214).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Adverse Decision of the Examiner (appealable action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally an Office action including a rejection of one or more claims. Appeal is taken from the Office action, so the Office action defines the Examiner’s position on appeal. You cannot appeal from every Office action — application must be twice rejected. The Office action does not have to be final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm appealability (two rejections) and that the appeal is from the correct Office action defining the Examiner's position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2: Notice of Appeal requirements and deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: You must give notice that you intend to appeal from the Examiner’s decision and pay an appeal fee. The notice and payment of the fee are due 3 months after the mailing date of the Examiner’s decision (extendable for 3 additional months; can file up to 6 months after the decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use USPTO form (link provided). Timeliness is critical — track mailing dates and extents precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 3: Appeal Brief filing deadline and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: No fee due with Appeal Brief. The Appeal Brief is due 2 months after you file the Notice of Appeal (extendable for 5 additional months). It is a legal brief (not a form) that includes your arguments and defines the appeal. The Appeal Brief identifies the issues the judges will consider on appeal; the judges generally will not go looking for issues — arguments not raised may be waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a comprehensive legal brief on the record; timely filing is subject to strict extension limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal Brief required contents
rubrics_metrics.description: No new evidence or substantive amendment. Must include certain sections: real party in interest; related matters (e.g., appeals, AIA proceedings, district court cases); summary of the claimed subject matter; argument; claims appendix. A pro se appellant needs to only 'substantially comply' with certain requirements shown in bold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all enumerated sections are present; avoid introducing new evidence or substantive amendments in the brief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal Brief argument formatting and content (37 C.F.R. § 41.37(c)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments of appellant with respect to each ground of rejection, and the basis therefor, with citations of the statutes, regulations, authorities, and parts of the Record relied on. The arguments shall explain why the examiner erred as to each ground of rejection contested by appellant. Except as provided in §§ 41.41, 41.47 and 41.52, any arguments or authorities not included in the appeal brief will be refused consideration by the Board for purposes of the present appeal. Each ground of rejection contested by appellant must be argued under a separate heading, and each heading shall reasonably identify the ground of rejection being contested (e.g., by claim number, statutory basis, and applied reference, if any).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure arguments under separate headings, include full citations, and anticipate that the Board will refuse to consider anything not included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 4: Examiner’s Answer content
rubrics_metrics.description: The Examiner’s response to the Appeal Brief. The Examiner will respond to all of the arguments in the Appeal Brief and will consider whether to maintain or modify each rejection. Includes sections: Ground(s) of Rejection to Be Reviewed on Appeal (Withdrawn Rejection(s); New Ground(s) of Rejection) and Response to Arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the Examiner to address each argument; New Grounds raised by Examiner may affect reply and hearing strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 5: Appeal Forwarding Fee (deadline and non-extendability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Due 2 months after Examiner’s Answer — NOT EXTENDABLE. May be filed with Reply Brief (optional) and/or request for oral hearing (optional). No fee for Reply Brief. Request for oral hearing requires payment of a fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not miss the non-extendable forwarding fee deadline; commonly forgotten and essential to move appeal forward to the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 5: Reply Brief (limitations and deadline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional. Due 2 months after Examiner’s Answer — NOT EXTENDABLE. Should be submitted at the same time as payment of the appeal forwarding fee. No additional fee for the Reply Brief. Only one Reply Brief permitted. No new evidence or amendment; no new arguments that were not raised in the Appeal Brief, unless responsive to an argument in the Examiner’s Answer or addressing new ground of rejection in the Examiner’s Answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit reply to responses permitted by rule; coordinate timing with forwarding fee and consider whether reply is strategically necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 5: Oral Hearing Request (deadline and fee)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional. Due 2 months after Examiner’s Answer or on the date of filing a Reply Brief, whichever is earlier — NOT EXTENDABLE. Must include payment of a fee. Office provides a form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely request and fee payment required if oral hearing is desired; consider whether oral argument will materially aid the appeal given judges will have read the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 6: Oral Hearing format and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If requested, attendance may be in person, telephonically, or via video. Decorum required. You will have 20 minutes to present your case to three judges, who may be in the hearing room or attending remotely. Judges will have already read the record on appeal and may or may not ask questions. No new arguments or evidence, absent a showing of good cause based on a recent, relevant decision of the PTAB or a Federal Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a concise 20-minute oral presentation focused on record-based arguments and be ready to answer judges' questions; new matters are generally barred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 7: Board Decision outcomes and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome may be an affirmance, an affirmance-in-part, a reversal, or new ground(s) of rejection. Affirmance: Each and every claim subject to a sustained rejection — no non-rejected claim. Affirmance-in-Part: At least one claim, but not all, subject to a sustained rejection. Reversed: No claim subject to a rejection — no sustained rejections. New Ground(s) of Rejection: The Judges issue a new rejection of one or more claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different outcomes have procedural consequences; understand classification of decision for next steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-decision responsibilities based on outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: If the outcome is an affirmance or new ground(s) of rejection, you must take the next step. If the outcome is an affirmance-in-part, you may take the next step. If the outcome is a reversal, the Examiner will take the next step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan post-decision strategy (RCE, amendment, request for rehearing, appeal to Federal Circuit) depending on the Board's disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Takeaway — ex parte appeals: what they provide and do not provide
rubrics_metrics.description: An ex parte appeal to the PTAB provides: a review by three judges, a more judicial forum, a determination as to whether the Examiner erred or not. An ex parte appeal does not: issue a patent, make a final determination as to patentability, prevent the application from returning to the Examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage expectations: appeal resolves the examiner's decision in the administrative record but does not grant patents or necessarily end prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic takeaway — evaluate need for patent protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether you need patent protection. Value is not necessarily the same as patentability. A patent conveys the right to exclude others from using the invention, not the right to use the invention. A patent is not required to commercialize the invention. Have you changed the invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider commercial and legal objectives before pursuing costly appeals or trials; changes in the invention may affect claims and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Takeaway — counsel recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not need a lawyer to appeal to the PTAB, but often having a lawyer is a good idea. The PTAB treats every appellant equally, and has publicly available resources to assure each appellant gets a fair shake, with or without a lawyer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available USPTO resources (PTAB website, Hearings Guide, MPEP, CFR) and consider counsel for complex appeals or AIA trials.
